text: Great, thank you, Mr. Lee. In terms of the second question about can councillors say they, do they truly represent the community? The councillors that I've worked with over the last four years work very hard on behalf of their community. They work very hard on this budget. We began working on this budget in November and spent many months working through the detail of the budget, the detail of the capital works programme, the challenges that we faced with the impact of COVID on the budget, the challenges where we incurred additional costs and lost revenue as a result of the COVID-19 virus and the challenges that we would face in expanding or in maintaining services in our community. There is a simple reality with the mechanics of a council budget. If you run at a deficit, then you build up debt or you run down your reserves and those reserves are there, they're hard earned. They are there to contribute to major capital works projects. So in years when we have a definite cash surplus, the cash surplus goes into reserves and then in subsequent years when we have major capital projects, the reserves are drawn upon to fund that capital works. For example, in the year when we had the basketball stadium built at Mullum Mullum Reserve, we had a very substantial building of around $20 million built. We drew on the capital reserves that have been built through cash surpluses. And through the reserves that are in the parks and reserves fund and develop contribution reserve funds. So the process of a council budget is very complex. It isn't as simple as just saying a number as a surplus and assuming that that's cash that the council has available, it's not how it works. And the councillors have been very judicious in ensuring that we have a balanced outcome. We have put a substantial $3 million fund on the table this coming financial year, in terms of our COVID response, that those funds are very carefully targeted to the people who are most in need in our community. It could have been done through a rate to not taking a 2% rate rise, but then we would have been in an even more difficult position in trying to provide services to those most at risk and most at need in our community. And the decision we took as a council was unanimous. It was to put in the 2% rise. It's an average impact of $36 per, an impact on an average of $36 per rate payer. That is a modest amount when spread over a year, it's less than a dollar a week. And that provided us millions of dollars to put into the community to those most in need and most under stress in the current environment. And we believe that that was an equitable and balanced outcome as a council. And is us representing the best interest of the entire community by providing support to those who are most in need. And for one, I am very proud of the decision the council made and the cohesive way that the councillors work towards that goal. Of course, the other challenge is, is if you start to cut revenue from council, you then have to start to pick and choose what services will you cut? Because in the end, council spends every one of its dollar on building community assets and on providing services into the community. And if you want to cut revenue of council, you have to cut services and have to cut employment because that's the other places that money goes. When we build things in the community, we spend that money on businesses in the community. If we don't build as much, we are reducing the actual economic activity in our city. So it is a very difficult balancing act that the councillors have to go through. But even then we managed to absorb millions of dollars worth of extra costs. We absorbed $750,000 worth of extra costs in waste charges, which are additional taxes placed on the council by the state government. Single source of that increase of $750,000 cost is increasing tax from the state government. We've absorbed that and we haven't passed that rise in costs onto the community.
